title: Is Everything Okay
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses what leaders should do when a normally reliable colleague suddenly slips into mediocrity or disengagement. It warns against the common instinct to confront the performance dip head-on, arguing that drastic behavioral shifts often trace back to a private crisis the person is reluctant to disclose. Instead of demanding an explanation, the author recommends a simple, caring question - is everything okay - as a way to open the door without forcing disclosure. The piece frames this as both more humane and more effective than direct confrontation, since it signals that the change has been noticed while leaving room for the employee to decide how much to share. It closes by tying the practice to a broader definition of good leadership as compassionate attentiveness.
points: Sudden drops in performance or attitude often stem from a personal crisis the employee hasn't disclosed, not laziness or defiance.
Directly confronting the behavior change can come across as insensitive if the real cause is a health issue, loss, or other hidden hardship.
Asking a simple, caring question - 'Is everything okay?' - invites disclosure without demanding it.
The question still works even when the cause is more mundane, like burnout or dissatisfaction with an assignment.
Presuming a personal crisis rather than jumping to judgment is the safer, more effective default for leaders.
quotes: Talented and productive colleagues sometimes take a left turn toward mediocrity and sub-par work without any plausible explanation.
This direct approach seems like the best course of action and most leaders take it — on many occasions, to their embarrassment.
Drastic shifts in performance often have an underlying cause unrelated to the workplace.
The better course of action is always to presume that a sizable shift in performance may be a result of a personal crisis and not a late-night TV binge.
Such a question opens the door for the colleague to share whatever they feel comfortable with.
Leaders of all stripes never know what they don’t know — especially about the personal issues that may be influencing workplace behavior.
The best bet is not to guess, but instead to inquire with compassion.
